newsitem.title: UK: Low jobless figures boost UK's Major.
newsitem.headline: Low jobless figures boost UK's Major.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, his party split and his parliamentary majority a thing of the past, received a boost on Wednesday when the jobless total fell below two million for the first time in six years.

In the largest monthly fall for a quarter of a century, the November jobless total declined by a much larger than expected 95,800 to 1.93 million, or 6.9 percent of the workforce, official figures showed.
"They are not good they are magnificent," Major said of the unemployment numbers.
Evidence of a pre-Christmas shopping boom came in the form of retail sales up by 0.7 percent, well above most experts' forecasts.

The figures were a lifeline for the ruling Conservatives, who face deep divisions over Britain's relations with Europe and the loss last week of their overall majority in the House of Commons following a by-election victory by the Labour Party.
Major is trailing badly in opinion polls but must call a general election no later than May next year. He is hoping improved economic conditions will win over voters by then.

Employment Secretary Gillian Shephard, while accepting that 20,000 of the fall in unemployment was accounted for by a work scheme which takes claimants off the jobless rolls, was as jubilant as the prime minister.

"Britain is now the only major European country with unemployment below two million, well below the 2.25 million in Spain, 2.75 million in Italy, three million in France and four million in Germany," she said.
Trade minister Ian Lang said: "Britain is the envy of Europe. Social burdens on business are destroying jobs in Europe, while Britain is creating them by the thousand."
Average earnings figures showed an increase of 4.0 percent in October, unchanged from the previous month.

While the figures were a boost for Major, whose government lost a vote in the House of Commons on Tuesday night, they raised the spectre of his being forced to announce a damaging rise in interest rates before the general election.
"Demand is strengthening and is going to continue to do so in the New Year, keeping the pressure on for higher base rates," said analyst Tom Rayner of Societe Generale.

The data suggested that a rise in the current base interest rate of 6.0 percent was likely in January of February, but Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke may try and keep a lid on rates until the general election, analysts said.
